mainText:
If you only remember one thing: Anthropic just named seven China-based A I labs, including Alibaba and Deep Seek, running large-scale campaigns to distill Claude's capabilities into their own models. That's landing right as Dario Amodei's slow-down essay has every major A I lab C E O publicly arguing about pacing.

Section one. A I developments.

OpenAI's G P T six Astra is rolling out to Pro and Enterprise users. President Greg Brockman says it's the first model to trip OpenAI's critical cybersecurity threshold, meaning it can find unknown security flaws and build exploits largely on its own. Built-in safeguards are the headline right alongside that capability jump.

Google shipped Gemini three point eight Live yesterday, undercutting rivals on voice pricing, half a cent per minute of audio in, under two cents per minute out.

Shanghai A I Lab released a huge open-weight model called Atria Dawn Preview, seven hundred forty four billion parameters, free to use under an M I T license. It edges out GPT five point six Sol on several benchmarks. Another sign of how fast Chinese open models are closing the gap.

From your Rundown newsletter: a ChatGPT co-creator, likely Mira Murati and John Schulman at Thinking Machines Lab, has been pushing a new kind of interaction model, built for live streaming voice, video, and text collaboration instead of the usual back and forth chat.

And Anthropic ended its temporary fifty percent weekly usage boost that's been in place since May, replacing it with a permanent twenty five percent bump over the original allowance. Worth knowing if your own Claude usage has shifted lately.

Why it matters: the model race and the safety conversation are now running on the same clock. Bigger capability jumps are arriving alongside bigger guardrail announcements.

Section two. A I ethics and policy.

Dario Amodei's essay asking frontier labs to slow down has pulled the C E Os of Microsoft, OpenAI, and X A I into a public argument over pacing. It's the first time this debate has played out openly among the people who actually control the roadmaps. Your Recode China A I newsletter is asking the obvious follow-up: will Chinese labs join a pause, or use it as an opening?

Anthropic's fourth threat intelligence report, published September tenth and flagged in your reads, named seven China-based labs, Alibaba, Moonshot, Deep Seek, Zhipu, Xiaomi, SenseTime, and MiniMax, running unauthorized distillation campaigns against Claude. Roughly one hundred ninety million exchanges total, more than one hundred fifty one million from Alibaba alone.

In California, Governor Newsom has until September thirtieth to sign or veto the Frontier A I Safety Act. Colorado is releasing formal audit rules for its own A I law. Brazil's Senate is voting today on a major A I regulation package. And the E U's A I Office has started technical audits on high-risk systems, while China's Cyberspace Administration is testing whether public generative tools embed both visible watermarks and hidden cryptographic metadata.

Why it matters: regulation is moving from paperwork to enforcement in multiple places at once, right as the industry's own safety debate goes public.

Section three. Tech geopolitics.

U S chip policy has quietly cooled. The Commerce Department is now approving higher-tier chip exports to China and leaning on enforcing existing rules rather than adding new restrictions, as the White House prioritizes trade stability. Nvidia's H two hundred chip now gets case-by-case review for China-bound exports, with third-party U S testing, a fifty percent volume cap, and a twenty five percent tariff, a real reversal from the earlier blanket-denial stance. Chip smuggling through Malaysia and Singapore remains widespread, and the old bipartisan consensus on China chip restrictions has fractured into a three-way standoff between Congress, the White House, and industry.

Why it matters: the chip choke point that shaped the last three years of the A I race is loosening right as model competition is heating up.

Section four. Tech for good.

From your Noosphere newsletter: an on-the-ground report from a girls' school in Afghanistan, documenting what may be the last year of education available to those students. That's the top of the news. Your full briefing is in the recording.
